questions.q: List the four women interlocutors from ancient texts whom Sen explicitly names as participants in India's argumentative tradition, and the textual source for each.
questions.a: Gargi (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad), Maitreyi (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad), Draupadi (Mahabharata / Kiratarjuniya), and Mira Bai (medieval Bhakti tradition). A wrong answer — such as listing only modern figures like Sarojini Naidu or omitting the textual source — reveals the student has not distinguished between ancient and modern evidence, a key distinction Sen makes to show historical depth.

questions.q: Sen writes: "Maitreyi's worldly worries might well have some transcendental relevance... but they certainly have worldly interest as well." Explain in your own words what "worldly interest" Sen derives from Maitreyi's question, and how he uses it in his own work on development economics.
questions.a: Maitreyi asks what use is wealth if it cannot grant immortality; Sen reads this as a critique of equating development with GDP growth alone. He uses it to argue that development must be assessed by expansion of human capabilities (living long, living well), not just income — the core of his "Development as Freedom" framework. A wrong answer that treats Maitreyi's question as purely spiritual misses Sen's deliberate secular, policy-relevant reinterpretation.

questions.q: Sen cites the Bhavisya Purana's genealogical argument against caste ("All human beings have the same father..."). Identify two other textual episodes Sen provides where caste hierarchy is challenged through argument, and name the speakers.
questions.a: (1) Bhrigu vs Bharadvaja in the Mahabharata — Bharadvaja points out skin-colour variation within castes and shared human emotions. (2) Medieval mystical poets — Kabir (weaver), Ravidas (shoemaker), Dadu (cotton-carder), Sena (barber) — who used verse to reject caste and religious barriers. A wrong answer that only names the Bhavisya Purana or lists poets without their occupations shows failure to track Sen's pattern: arguments from lived experience of the marginalized.

questions.q: Compare Sen's treatment of the Krishna-Arjuna debate (Gita) with his treatment of the Draupadi-Yudhisthira exchange (Kiratarjuniya). How does the second exchange complicate the "message of the Gita" that Sen discusses?
questions.a: The Gita presents Krishna's deontological duty (fare forward) as ultimately victorious, but Sen notes Arjuna's consequentialist doubts remain powerful. Draupadi's speech goes further: she actively mocks Yudhisthira's pacifism as unmanly and demands heroic action, aligning with the "fare forward" impulse but from a woman's voice and with political urgency. This complicates the Gita's message by showing (a) women could advocate the "duty" side more aggressively than men, and (b) the epic itself stages multiple, conflicting moral perspectives — not a single univocal teaching. A wrong answer that says "Draupadi supports Krishna" misses the gendered, political dimension Sen highlights.

questions.q: Sen warns against "twin pitfalls" regarding democracy in India. Evaluate which pitfall is more dangerous for a student writing a board exam answer on "roots of Indian democracy," and justify your choice with reference to the text.
questions.a: The first pitfall — seeing democracy as merely a British gift — is more dangerous for exam answers because it leads to a factually incomplete, Eurocentric narrative that ignores Sen's evidence: ancient traditions of public reasoning (Upanishads, epics, Buddhist councils), heterodoxy as norm, and the Constituent Assembly drawing on *both* Western institutions and indigenous argumentative culture. The second pitfall (Indian exceptionalism) is also wrong but less likely in a standard answer. A student who only credits British influence will lose marks for "critical thinking" and "appreciation" criteria that demand textual evidence from Sen.

questions.q: Write a 150-word paragraph in Sen's argumentative style, using at least three pieces of textual evidence from the essay, to defend the claim: "India's argumentative tradition has always been a resource for the marginalized, not just the elite."
questions.a: A strong answer weaves together: Gargi's "militant" questioning of Yajnavalkya (Upanishad), Bharadvaja's empirical demolition of caste-by-colour (Mahabharata), and the medieval poet-craftsmen (Kabir, Ravidas, Dadu, Sena) whose verses attacked caste and religious barriers from working-class experience. It notes Sen's explicit statement: "Some of the most powerful arguments... have been about the lives of the least privileged groups." A weak answer lists names without showing *how* each example supports the claim, or omits the medieval poets — missing Sen's class-based evidence.
